newsitem.title: USA: Texas standoff ends without a shot.
newsitem.headline: Texas standoff ends without a shot.

text.p: A week-long standoff between police and armed Texas separatists ended without a shot on Saturday when the rebel leader gave up his vow to fight to the death and surrendered.

Republic of Texas "ambassador" Richard McLaren, his wife and three followers, surrounded by elite police units, walked out of their mountain compound and into what promises to be a long legal battle after signing a ceasefire agreement that McLaren appeared to view as a victory.
The rebels, who say that Texas is an independent nation, held a military ceremony where they laid down their guns before giving themselves up to police.

McLaren and the others were taken to Presidio County Jail in nearby Marfa, Texas where he smiled and waved the agreement at a phalanx of reporters as he was driven by. The Republic members face a battery of federal and state charges in the siege, which began on Sunday when they took two hostages in retaliation for the arrest by local police of security chief Robert Scheidt on weapons charges.

Police patted themselves on the back for reaching a peaceful conclusion to the saga, but there was still work to be done. Two of the rebels chose not to surrender and fled into the surrounding Davis Mountains where helicopters, bloodhounds and troopers on horses searched for them.

The end to the tense siege came a few hours after McLaren's wife, Evelyn, left the rebels' tin-walled compound and surrendered. She told police the remaining Republic members were ready to turn themselves in.

Texas Department of Public Safety spokesman Mike Cox said McLaren, who talked tough throughout the ordeal and vowed to never surrender, was convinced to give up by the dozens of heavily-armed police who on Friday night had moved within a quarter-mile of what he called "the embassy."
"He was very much aware we had a very strong presence around his area," Cox said.

McLaren, a 43-year-old vintner from Missouri, had shown little willingness to surrender until the Friday night deployment. As the police moved in, he shouted out on shortwave radio an international "Mayday" call and told police: "We'll take a good hunk of you boys with us."

Estimates of up to 200 police poured into the area to surround the separatists' compound, backed by armoured personnel carriers, military helicopters, battering rams and bomb disposal equipment which Cox said would be used to defuse explosives planted by the separatists.

McLaren was to be arraigned on Saturday night before local Justice of the Peace Cinderella Gonzalez. Along with charges related to the kidnapping, he and wife Evelyn will face federal tax and fraud charges.

The siege ended a dispute that had been brewing for four months since McLaren defied a federal judge's order to appear in court in a dispute about the many bogus liens and other legal papers he filed in the name of the Republic of Texas.
He and his followers had holed up in their compound, actually a mobile home, defying police to arrest them.

Attorney Terence O'Rourke, who represented the McLarens in the tortuous negotiations leading to the siege's end, said McLaren was happy because the ceasefire agreement included recognition of the Republic of Texas and a guarantee that he could argue before a federal judge in Washington D.C. that there should be a referendum on the issue of Texas independence.

The Republic of Texas, which claims to have thousands of members and ties to anti-government militia groups, says that Texas' 1845 annexation by the United States was illegal. Texas was an independent nation for nine years after it broke from Mexico in 1936.
But police indicated that the agreement might not be worth as much as McLaren thought.
"There is no agreement other than they agreed to come out peacefully and they agreed to cease fire," Cox said. "There were no promises on the part of the Department of Public Safety."
Nonetheless, O'Rourke said the agreement was sufficient to stop a possible bloodbath. "They (police) were ready to push the button. It was a now or never situation."
Scheidt, who surrendered on Friday, told reporters on Saturday as he was taken to the Marfa jail the rebel group had given up because "patriots don't win battles any more."
But, he vowed, "This is just the beginning of the Republic of Texas."

Texas Gov. George W. Bush, in a news conference in Austin, said the Republic of Texas group was free to exist, but within limits. "You're fine holding any views you want in Texas as long as you don't up and start to hurt someone."
